title: TypeScript with React
summary: Typing props, children and defaults, state and refs, event handlers, generic components, discriminated unions for props, and typing context and reducers.

sections.title: Props
sections.body:
Type props with a `type` or `interface` and destructure in the parameter: `function Button({ label, onClick }: ButtonProps)`. Optional props use `?` and get defaults in the destructuring. Use `React.ReactNode` for anything renderable, including `children`; `React.ReactElement` (or `JSX.Element`) only when you need an element specifically.

To accept all the props of a DOM element, extend `React.ComponentProps<"button">` (or `ComponentPropsWithoutRef`) and spread the rest.

sections.title: State, refs and events
sections.body:
`useState` infers from the initial value; give a type when it starts empty or nullable: `useState<User | null>(null)`, `useState<string[]>([])`.

DOM refs: `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)` gives a `RefObject<HTMLInputElement | null>`; check for `null` before use. Mutable value refs: `useRef<number | null>(null)`.

Events: `React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`, `React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>`, `React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>`, `React.KeyboardEvent`. Inline handlers infer the type, so annotate only when the handler is defined separately.

sections.title: Generic components
sections.body: A component can be generic, like a function: `function List<T>({ items, render }: { items: T[]; render: (item: T) => React.ReactNode })`. TypeScript infers `T` from `items` at the call site. In a `.tsx` file an arrow function needs `<T,>` so the parser does not read `<T>` as a JSX tag.

sections.title: Unions for props and actions
sections.body:
A **discriminated union** makes impossible prop combinations impossible: `type Props = { status: "loading" } | { status: "error"; error: string } | { status: "ok"; data: Item[] }`. After checking `status`, TypeScript narrows to the right shape. The same pattern types reducer actions and makes `switch` exhaustive.

Type a context with its value or `null`, and export a hook that throws when the provider is missing, so callers get a non-null type.

pitfalls: `useState(null)` without a type, which infers `null` forever.
Using `React.FC` and expecting implicit `children` (removed from `FC` in React 18 types).
Typing `children` as `JSX.Element`, which rejects strings and arrays.
Writing `<T>() =>` in a `.tsx` file instead of `<T,>() =>`.

gotchas.question: What type should `children` usually have?
gotchas.answer: `React.ReactNode`, which covers elements, strings, numbers, arrays, `null` and booleans.

gotchas.question: What does `useState(null)` infer without a type argument?
gotchas.answer: `null`, so you cannot later set an object. Write `useState<User | null>(null)`.
